problem: The sentence 'Swapping the two for clauses changes the order of the results' is not true for the example just given. With [i + j for i in range(1, 3) for j in range(1, 3)] both clauses walk 1, 2 and addition is commutative, so the swapped line [i + j for j in range(1, 3) for i in range(1, 3)] also prints [2, 3, 3, 4]. A student who tries it will think the book is wrong.
fix: Use an example where the order really shows, e.g. [i + j for i in range(1, 3) for j in range(1, 4)] gives [2, 3, 4, 3, 4, 5] while [i + j for j in range(1, 4) for i in range(1, 3)] gives [2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5], and say 'swapping the clauses can change the order of the results'.

problem: 'Set and dictionary comprehensions reuse the same pattern with braces and a key-value pair' is wrong for set comprehensions. A set comprehension is {expr for item in iterable} with no key-value pair; only a dictionary comprehension has the key: value form.
fix: 'Set comprehensions use the same pattern with braces in place of brackets: {expr for item in iterable}. Dictionary comprehensions add a key-value pair: {k: v for item in iterable}. Both are covered in 3.6 Dictionaries and 3.7 Sets.'
